## Which axle should Pybricks count? {#gear-setup data-cue="gear-setup" data-chapter="1 / The mechanism" data-phase="Code"}

::: {.lab-slot}
:::

::: {.notes}
Recall the 12-tooth motor gear and 20-tooth output gear from Gears. Read the constructor from left to right: Port E, the motor's positive direction, then the gear train from motor to output. Pybricks scales subsequent angle and speed commands to the 20-tooth output axle. Its positive direction still describes the motor shaft; on this build, positive closes the claw. The label on the simulation says “Home not set” until the open stop is found and named zero in chapter 3. Source: https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html
:::

## Find an angle that grips {#grip-lab data-cue="grip-lab" data-chapter="4 / The angle lab" data-phase="Try it"}

::: {.lab-slot}
:::

::: {.notes}
One scripted comparison instead of six slides. Ask for a prediction before each trial: the button names the trial it is about to run. Every completed trial stays in the table, which is what makes the comparison visible.

The claw was homed with empty jaws, then this wide object was placed between the open jaws. The program requests the same 45° output target demonstrated in stage 3, measured from home. The dotted outline marks that requested destination. Ask whether the jaws will touch the object there.

Nothing blocked the movement, so the jaws reach the requested 45° and hold it. A gap remains. This target is too small for this object. Ask what number to request instead.

Only the requested output target changes, from 45 to 60. The same object and the same home reference are kept. The dotted outline now sits inside the object. Predict the angle the jaws will report when the movement ends.

Both jaws meet the object near 52°. The requested target stays 60° while the actual output angle stops near 52°, and the motor task is still trying toward the destination it never reached. Contact here does not measure holding force on a real robot. Keep 60° for the next trial.

The requested target stays 60°, homed from the same reference. Only the object is narrower. Predict whether the jaws stop early again or reach the requested destination.

Nothing blocks this movement. The jaws arrive at the requested 60° and a gap remains, the same result the 45° trial gave with the wide object. The number that worked before does not work here.
:::

## Each object has its own contact angle {#contact-explain data-cue="contact-explain" data-chapter="4 / The angle lab" data-phase="Explain"}

::: {.lab-slot}
:::

::: {.notes}
Three trials, one requested number each: 45° left a gap, 60° was stopped by the wide object near 52°, and the same 60° left a gap on the narrower one. Picking an exact angle for every object is impractical. Ask what the claw would need to notice instead of counting degrees.

## Could the program recognize blocked movement? {#detect-blockage data-cue="detect-blockage" data-chapter="5 / Resistance and home()" data-phase="Predict"}

::: {.lab-slot}
:::

::: {.notes}
Recall an experiment in which the object stopped the jaws before the target. Then recall *Stop at the Wall*: the wheels already told us when a wall blocked them. Predict what evidence the claw's motor could give the same way.

Run closing until blocked. Ask what the motor is still being asked to do. Explain that the controller can detect a stall when movement is obstructed.
:::

## stalled() reports blocked movement {#stall-reveal data-cue="stall-reveal" data-chapter="5 / Resistance and home()" data-phase="Code"}

::: {.lab-slot}
:::

::: {.notes}
Students met `stalled()` at the wall in *Stop at the Wall* (`drive_to_wall`, `wall_square`); this is the same flag on the claw motor, so name it as a recap and don't re-teach it. What is new here is its live indicator, and the reading below. It reports the controller stall detection, not what caused the blockage. Source: https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html#pybricks.pupdevices.Motor.stalled

Press once more for the reading this stage exists to establish: a stall reports blocked movement, not a held object. The object here caused it; the next slide shows the rigid open stop causing the same report with nothing to catch. Stage 9 tries a checking loop on exactly this reading before trading it for a faster one, and stage 10 returns to what a finished loop leaves unknown.
:::

## How did home() recognize the open stop? {#home-detection data-cue="home-detection" data-chapter="5 / Resistance and home()" data-phase="Predict"}

::: {.lab-slot}
:::

::: {.notes}
Connect this to the function students already used. home() is still folded. Let them propose using the blockage at the open stop, then open the function and read it one line at a time. Each line answers a question, and every line is revealed just above the line it protects.

Reveal claw.run_until_stalled and run it to the stall event at the rigid stop. It is the instruction inside their own `drive_to_wall` from *Stop at the Wall*, now pushing jaws into a stop instead of wheels into a wall. This one instruction performs the running and the stall checking; students do not need to write a loop. It answers the slide question. Source: https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html#pybricks.pupdevices.Motor.run_until_stalled

Ask how hard the motor should push into the stop before pressing. The effort limit appears above the run, because a setting has to be chosen before the instruction that uses it. The supplied homing limit is 220 mNm, which caps how hard the motor may try. The last reveal compares the effort limits here, where the function uses them.

Ask which familiar instruction gives the stop the number zero. Let students answer before revealing reset_angle. The operation finishes and coasts, then the angle is set to 0. The jaws do not move: finding the stop supplies the physical reference, and resetting the angle labels it zero. The live stall indicator can clear once drive effort is released; the previous stall event remains the evidence.

Ask why a line that does nothing sits above the zeroing. After the coast the motor is still coming to rest, so 200 ms guarantees the number we record is the settled one. Our closing angles are found by practice runs rather than calculation, which only works if zero lands in the same place every run.

Ask whether the raised limit should stay raised. Limits persist, so home() explicitly restores the gripping limit before returning; watch the torque reading change. The jaws remain fully open at zero, and there is no further movement in home(). Open Home code to read the finished function.

Both limit lines are marked together with their values. Ask what controls how hard the motor may try, and compare the homing limit 220 mNm with the gripping limit 180 mNm: reaching the rigid stop is allowed more effort than gripping an object. A setting stays in effect until it is changed, which is why each action selects its own. The torque limit is a motor setting in mNm; this model does not measure jaw-tip force.
:::

## When will “Continue” appear? {#empty data-cue="empty" data-chapter="7 / Default waiting" data-phase="Predict"}

::: {.lab-slot}
:::

::: {.notes}
Stage 7 follows the reference, experiment, and resistance lessons. The empty claw starts homed at the rigid open stop. Positive motor rotation closes this build. The runner supplies a gripping limit of 180 mNm. Keep stalled() visible as a familiar indicator from stage 5; done() will be introduced in stage 9. Ask when the second message will print, and take predictions aloud. Next runs the scene. Geometry and contact angles are illustrative, not calibrated robot measurements.

Let the animation finish. Follow the jaws, the pending call, and the target readout. It freezes after the second print. Playback is slowed without changing the speed constants. A presentation pause freezes model time; it does not send a motor stop command.

Ask students to explain the order: closing starts, 72° at the output is reached, then the second print executes. Stop.HOLD maintains the reached target. Reference: https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html#pybricks.pupdevices.Motor.run_target
:::

## What changes when we add an object? {#blocked data-cue="blocked" data-chapter="7 / Default waiting" data-phase="Predict"}

::: {.lab-slot}
:::

::: {.notes}
The starting angle, target, speed, and Python code are unchanged. Only the object changes. Ask when the second print will appear now.

The presentation freezes after blockage is detected. The Python call remains pending: we have not made it time out or return. Navigating to a fresh trial resets the scene.

Ask: We reached the object. What is the program still waiting for? Compare actual output angle near 52° with target 72°. The second message has not printed. Contact does not satisfy target arrival.
:::

## The default is wait=True {#default-argument data-cue="default-argument" data-chapter="7 / Default waiting" data-phase="Code"}

::: {.lab-slot}
:::

::: {.notes}
Make the implicit default visible. Adding wait=True here states the same behavior as omitting it. This is *Name Your Moves*' "knob with a default" from the other side: they wrote defaults into their own verbs, and Pybricks wrote this one into `run_target`. Ask them to say it in D5's words ("a factory setting you can override for one call") rather than explaining it again.
:::

## What will wait=False change? {#async data-cue="async" data-chapter="8 / Let the program continue" data-phase="Predict"}

::: {.lab-slot}
:::

::: {.notes}
The trial resets and only the waiting argument changes. The program is now three instructions long: print, the closing command, print. Ask when the second message will print, and then ask what the program will do after that.

The second message appears immediately, while the jaws are barely open. wait=False let the program continue instead of waiting for arrival.

Press again. There is nothing left to run, so the program ends. Ending a program releases the motors, and the jaws stop at about 2° with 72° still the requested angle. Ask what the program achieved: it issued a closing command and then took it away. The motor was never given time to work. The simulator's instruction ticks are illustrative, not firmware timing.
:::

## How long should the program wait? {#fixed-wait data-cue="fixed-wait" data-chapter="8 / Let the program continue" data-phase="Predict"}

::: {.lab-slot}
:::

::: {.notes}
The program needs to stay alive while the motor works, so we add a wait. Someone has to choose the number, and 200 ms sounds reasonable. Ask how far the jaws will get, and take a show of hands before running it.

The countdown beside the line runs out and the program ends with the output near 25°. The wide object would stop it near 52°, so this trial ended before the claw touched anything. Nobody measured how long the closing takes; the number was a guess and the guess was short.

Ask the obvious follow-up: how much longer should it be? Any answer is another guess, and it changes with the object, the speed, and how far the jaws start from the target. Worse, a wait that is long enough still tells us nothing, because it measures time and never looks at the motor. We need to wait for the motor instead.
:::

## What could tell us the closing is over? {#load-loop data-cue="load-loop" data-chapter="9 / The checking loop" data-phase="Predict"}

::: {.lab-slot}
:::

::: {.notes}
Take answers before revealing any code. Recall stalled() from stage 5: it reports that the motor is being asked to move and cannot continue. Ask how a program could use it to decide when to stop waiting.

The next press replaces the fixed wait with a loop: keep waiting while the motor is not stalled. Read it aloud. wait(100) gives the movement time to begin before the first check, and wait(10) spaces the checks; neither cancels the motor task. These supplied intervals are not guarantees for every physical build. The observation wait that keeps the scene alive is left out of this excerpt.

Run it, and watch the jaws and the check counter together. The jaws stop at the object, but the loop keeps checking for a while before stalled() turns True. stalled() only reports once the motor has pushed at its full 180 mNm limit for a moment, and the last part of that push builds slowly. The loop works: the second message appears because the closing attempt is over, not because a chosen number of milliseconds elapsed. But grab() would sit still with the jaws already on the object. Ask what the motor could tell us sooner.

Press again. The loop now reads claw.load(): how hard the motor is pushing, in mNm. Closing on air it reads a small number, the gear friction. Pressing on the object it climbs toward the 180 limit, and the loop leaves as it passes 100, on the way up. The closing command is still running, so the squeeze keeps rising to 180 after the loop ends. load() reads negative while closing, which is why the code wraps it in abs(). The 100 must sit above the closing-on-air reading and below the 180 limit: the load can never exceed the limit, so a limit at or below 100 would never end the loop on an object. Tune it by printing abs(claw.load()) while closing empty and on an object. The length of the pause in this model is illustrative.

stalled() is still the right tool in home(): there the full push into the rigid stop is exactly what we want to find.
:::

## Where will empty jaws stop? {#done-check data-cue="done-check" data-chapter="9 / The checking loop" data-phase="Predict"}

::: {.lab-slot}
:::

::: {.notes}
The same program with an empty claw. The requested output target stays at 72°, which is deliberately short of the angle where empty jaws would meet. Ask two questions before running: where will the jaws stop, and what will end the loop?

The jaws reach the requested 72° and stop there, with a visible gap still between them. Nothing is between the jaws, so nothing ever pushes back: the load stays at the small closing-on-air value, then drops once the jaws arrive, while the check counter keeps climbing against a motor that has already finished moving. Point at the gap. The movement succeeded and the claw is holding nothing.

Reveal claw.done(): it reports that the commanded movement has completed. It is the only ending available in this trial, because an unobstructed movement never builds load. On real hardware Pybricks decides completion using both position and speed tolerances, so a finished movement can rest a fraction of a degree from the requested angle; this model lands on the target exactly and does not simulate a controller.

With both checks, the loop ends on done() in this empty trial and still ends on the load when an object blocks the jaws. Ask the last question: the loop ended, so is an object held? Here done() is True at the requested 72°, with a gap between the jaws. Completion alone does not confirm a catch.

If a student proposes raising the 72° close target until the empty jaws do meet, follow it through. The trial would then end on the load instead, but every empty grab would end by grinding the jaws into each other at the torque limit, and done() could never become True because the movement never completes. The target is kept short of that on purpose. The cost is the other half of the trade: an object narrower than the remaining gap is never gripped at all, which is the same tuning question stage 4 raised.

References: https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html#pybricks.pupdevices.Motor.done and https://docs.pybricks.com/en/stable/pupdevices/motor.html#pybricks.pupdevices.Motor.control.target_tolerances
:::

## Either True ends the loop {#truth-table data-cue="truth-table" data-chapter="9 / The checking loop" data-phase="Explain"}

<div class="truth-layout"><pre class="condition"><code>while abs(claw.load()) &lt; 100 and not claw.done():</code></pre><table class="truth-table"><thead><tr><th>abs(load()) &gt;= 100</th><th>done()</th><th>Our checking loop</th></tr></thead><tbody><tr class="keep step"><td>False</td><td>False</td><td>Keep waiting</td></tr><tr class="step"><td>True</td><td>False</td><td>Leave the loop</td></tr><tr class="step"><td>False</td><td>True</td><td>Leave the loop</td></tr><tr class="step"><td>True</td><td>True</td><td>Leave the loop</td></tr></tbody></table></div>

::: {.notes}
This is the *Line King* truth table on a claw, so let students read the rows before you do. `abs(load) < 100` is the same as `not (abs(load) >= 100)`, so the condition is still `not A and not B`, which reads "neither has happened yet". That is why **either** True ends the loop: the `or` card from that session. Work through each row. Only False/False continues, which is exactly the two trials just run: the blocked object left on row two, the empty claw on row three. This table explains the Boolean expression; it does not claim all four combinations necessarily occur in this model.
:::

## What will an opening command change? {#release data-cue="release" data-chapter="10 / The three functions" data-phase="Predict"}

::: {.lab-slot}
:::

::: {.notes}
The object is held after the checking loop: the output is near 52° from home, the closing command is still active, and the effort limit is 180 mNm. Read the displayed command aloud and take predictions before running it.

The jaws open to 0° and the object is free. Point out that the opening command replaced the closing task; nothing had to cancel the earlier instruction first.

This sequence is release(). It has the same shape as the closing sequence: choose the effort limit, then run to a target. Default waiting is right here, because the next mission action follows arrival. Stage 11 asks how far it should actually open.
:::

## The three functions {#functions data-cue="functions" data-chapter="10 / The three functions" data-phase="Code"}

<div class="function-trio"><div class="step"><h3>home()</h3><pre><code>def home():
    claw.control.limits(
        torque=220)
    claw.run_until_stalled(
        speed=-120,
        then=Stop.COAST)
    wait(200)
    claw.reset_angle(angle=0)
    claw.control.limits(
        torque=180)</code></pre><p class="detail">The built-in operation ends, then coasts.</p></div><div class="step"><h3>grab()</h3><pre><code>def grab():
    claw.control.limits(
        torque=180)
    claw.run_target(
        speed=120,
        target_angle=72,
        then=Stop.HOLD,
        wait=False)
    wait(100)
    while (abs(claw.load()) &lt; 100
           and not claw.done()):
        wait(10)</code></pre><p class="detail">Our loop ends. The closing task keeps squeezing.</p></div><div class="step"><h3>release()</h3><pre><code>def release(angle=0):
    claw.control.limits(
        torque=180)
    claw.run_target(
        speed=180,
        target_angle=angle,
        then=Stop.COAST)</code></pre><p class="detail">The opening reaches its target, then coasts.</p></div></div>

::: {.notes}
Package everything the class has built. Reveal the three in order and read what ends each one, which is the line under each function.

home() and release() both wait for their own movement to finish. grab() cannot, because the movement it starts may never reach its target, so it starts the command with wait=False and watches for either outcome.

That difference has a consequence worth saying aloud: leaving our checking loop does not cancel the motor instruction. The closing command is still active while grab() returns, which is what keeps the object squeezed and lets the push keep rising from 100 to the 180 limit while the robot drives, and then=Stop.HOLD is what maintains the position if the target is actually reached. Demonstration prints and observation waits stay outside the functions. A return means one of the two conditions occurred; it does not certify a catch. This ends the excerpt covering stages 7-10.
:::

::: {.notes}
Students work independently before discussing answers. Run both trials on the bench build: home with the jaws empty, then place the object before grabbing, and repeat with nothing between the jaws.

home() finishes its built-in stalled movement, coasts, settles, sets zero, and restores the gripping limit. grab() returns when the load passes 100 mNm or done() becomes True. release() returns after its opening movement completes. An empty grab may finish on done() with no object held. Students should use the observed readings to explain both trials.

For a bench extension, use the same module on the supplied Port E build. Keep the homing path empty and adapt the marked TUNE settings to the physical mechanism. The completed download defines functions without starting a motion sequence. Run the operations under the instructor's guidance, placing the object after homing. The readings in the lesson are illustrative.
:::
